Point Solutions vs. One Platform: The Real Cost of Property Management Software

Should you run your whole property management company on one platform, or stack a handful of best-in-class point solutions around a core system? I've built RL Property Management the second way, on purpose. Steven Rea, Chief Innovation Officer at North Point (5,000+ doors across dozens of markets), spent the last several months tearing his stack down and rebuilding it the first way. In my podcast episode with Steven, we spent an hour going back and forth on it, and by the end neither of us had fully convinced the other.

Why North Point Ripped a Maintenance Platform Back Out

Steven's software philosophy comes from two very different chapters of his career. Early on, at what became RPM Living, the company ran entirely on Yardi - one login, one system, and every new hire learned the same way. When he later helped build out a startup studio's property management arm, the opposite happened: a different point solution for every function, and training became the job instead of a part of it. As he put it, "we spent most of our training time teaching people how to use software and not how to be great property managers."

When Steven landed at North Point, he inherited AppFolio "in name only." The team had migrated onto it from a different core system but was actually operating out of a separate maintenance platform and Power BI, so nobody trusted the data sitting in AppFolio because nobody was using it day to day. His fix was to strip it back down: North Point went from 27 different tools to six, folding maintenance coordination back into the core system on purpose, even though he says the maintenance platform he removed is genuinely good software. For him, the win was training simplicity now and a cleaner data foundation for what AI tooling can do once it's mapped against a single system instead of stitched together across several.

My Take: A Point Solution Earns Its Cost When It's a Clean Break

I don't run RL that way, and the conversation clarified for me why. We use [software note: transcript says "Building," most likely Buildium - flagged below] as our core, and we layer specialty tools around it for leasing and tenant screening, maintenance coordination, and rent comps. My framework is what I think of as a clean break: leasing is genuinely disconnected from day-to-day operations, so it's fine for it to live in its own system before a tenant moves in and we bring them into the core platform. Maintenance coordination is different : the work itself is physical, but the back-and-forth between tenant, owner, property manager, and vendor is exactly where a dedicated tool saves real time.

The cost argument doesn't move me much either way. If a tool lets my team manage 300 doors with one maintenance coordinator instead of 100, I'll pay two or three dollars a door for that every single time - that's not close. Where I think the real conversation belongs is whether a given tool actually delivers on that promise, and what you lose when your operational data lives in five different places instead of one. Steven's right that the second part has a cost that never shows up on a P&L. I just don't think the answer is always "put everything in one box."

Where I Pushed Back: Do Owners Deserve Below-Market Repair Pricing?

This is where Steven and I landed in genuinely different places. He's investing real time into shaving minutes off every maintenance visit at North Point - grouping work orders by zip code so techs aren't crisscrossing a market, building an integration with Home Depot and Lowe's so materials are waiting at the pro desk instead of being shopped for on-site. Owners are billed time-and-materials there, so those saved minutes flow straight through to them.

I think it's overbuilt for what it delivers. My position is that an owner paying a modest monthly management fee isn't entitled to institutional-grade repair pricing just because they've hired a property manager. I think about vendor pricing in three tiers: rip-off pricing from the private-equity-backed roll-ups, fair pricing from an established local pro, and unrealistic Home Depot parking lot pricing that nobody should expect. I aim for the middle tier, and that's the deal - not the same rate North Point's institutional clients get through sheer density. A 5–10% swing on a repair bill isn't something most retail owners even notice, and I'm not going to spend my team's time chasing it.

Steven's counter is that it was never really about the dollar amount. He's optimizing for trust and perception as much as the invoice total, and he thinks it compounds into retention and referrals over time, plus a lot of this infrastructure is really being built for North Point's institutional clients, who evaluate cost-to-maintain as a primary metric. Fair point. I still don't think most property managers should be spending their time here. Where do you land on it?

Rethinking the Fee Model: Leasing, Retention, and Who You Work With

The incentive conversation was the most useful part of the episode for me. At RL, we don't charge a leasing fee at all - we charge a lease renewal fee instead, on purpose, because I think a leasing fee rewards a property manager for filling a vacancy fast, not for finding the right tenant and keeping them. Steven landed in a similar place from a completely different direction: he'd like to invert the typical multifamily model and charge less for leasing, more for retention, because renewals are what actually protects an owner's cash flow over a full year.

He's also negotiating NOI-based management fees with a few institutional clients, with taxes, insurance, and capital expenditures carved out so the number reflects operating performance rather than one-time events. I've experimented with variations on this idea myself, and I always run into the same wall: an owner who underinvests in the property tanks its market position in ways that hurt my performance without my having any control over it, and an owner who overspends on cosmetic upgrades eats into a shared profit pool the same way. Chase that alignment far enough and you eventually conclude the only way to fully align the incentives is to just own the properties yourself.

What we agreed on, coming at it from opposite directions, is that client selection probably matters more than any fee formula. Steven described a "no asshole policy" from earlier in his career (firing clients who weren't paying bills or wouldn't invest in habitability, regardless of door count). I feel the same way about owners who treat every dollar I make as a dollar that should've been theirs. No formula fixes a relationship that was never going to work.

The Takeaway?

Software, pricing, and incentive design all circle back to the same tension: how much complexity is actually worth the return, and for which clients. Steven and I answered that question differently on tools and on maintenance pricing, and landed in nearly the same place on incentives and who's worth working with. I don't think there's one right answer here — I think the discipline is knowing which problems are actually worth solving for the business you're trying to build.
